22:7.text: In their heat I will make their feasts, and I will make them drunken, that they may rejoice, and sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake, saith the LORD.

provenance.other: “Make them drunken” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 51:39, and “sleep a perpetual sleep” occurs in exactly two, Jeremiah 51:39 and 51:57, which are the same oracle saying the same thing twice. Mosiah 22:7's “when they are drunken and asleep” pairs the two states, and the pairing is confined in the KJV to those two verses; drunkenness elsewhere in scripture (Nabal, Elah, Benhadad, Belshazzar) ends in a killing, not in a sleep that lets somebody slip away.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 51 is the oracle against Babylon, and the two things it promises are the two things Gideon's plan requires. God will make the garrison drunk and put it to sleep — “I will make drunk her princes, and her wise men, her captains, and her rulers, and her mighty men: and they shall sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake” — and while that is happening his people are to get out: “My people, go ye out of the midst of her, and deliver ye every man his soul.” Mosiah 22 is that oracle executed as a stratagem. What the borrowing does is assign the agency. In Jeremiah the drunkenness is the LORD's doing and the escape is a command; here the drunkenness is procured with a tribute of wine and some extra sent as a present, and the escape is a plan carried by a vote. The chapter takes a prophecy of divine judgment and stages it with a wine delivery — which is either the most secular sentence in the Limhi narrative or a claim that providence works through the tribute schedule, and the catalogue does not have to choose.

22:7.note: “I will go according to thy command, and pay the last tribute of wine to the Lamanites, and they will be drunken; and we will pass through the secret pass on the left of the camp, when they are drunken and asleep.” The KJV pairs drunkenness with a sleep that permits escape in exactly one place, the Babylon oracle of Jeremiah 51, where “I will make them drunken” is a singleton and the resulting “perpetual sleep” is repeated at 51:57 over the whole garrison — princes, captains, rulers, mighty men — and where the accompanying instruction to God's people is to go out of the midst of her and deliver every man his soul. That is the plan of this chapter, down to the order of its two halves. Recorded at moderate because Mosiah reproduces no clause; the case is that the combination is Jeremiah's alone.

22:8.text: And Moses said, We will go with our young and with our old, with our sons and with our daughters, with our flocks and with our herds will we go; for we must hold a feast unto the LORD.

provenance.other: “Our flocks and with our herds” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 10:9, as does “with our young and with our old” in the same verse; “flocks and your herds” occurs in exactly two, Exodus 10:24 and Exodus 12:32, both of them Pharaoh's side of the same negotiation. Mosiah 22:8's “our flocks and our herds” drops the repeated preposition and so is not a verbatim run, which is why the row is filed at moderate rather than higher.
provenance.significance: Exodus 10:9-11 and 10:24-26 are the KJV's one negotiation over the manifest of an escape: Moses insists on taking the young, the old, the sons, the daughters, the flocks and the herds, and Pharaoh's counter-offers are to keep the little ones, then to keep the livestock. The inventory is the argument. Mosiah 22:2 and 22:8 answer the same question in the same terms — women, children, flocks, herds, tents — and answer it Moses's way, all of it goes. The difference is who is asked. In Exodus the list has to be extracted from the oppressor; here it is settled by the voice of the people at 22:1 and by a captain's plan, and the Lamanites are not consulted because they are being got drunk. Reading the two together makes 22:10's tribute of wine the substitute for the plagues: the concession Pharaoh had to be beaten into is here simply bought.

22:8.note: “Thus we will depart with our women and our children, our flocks and our herds, into the wilderness.” The KJV's manifest for a departure of this kind is Exodus 10:9, where “with our flocks and with our herds will we go” closes a list of exactly these categories and is the point Pharaoh spends two more exchanges trying to whittle down. Mosiah reproduces the items and the first-person future — “we will go”, “we will depart” — but not the repeated preposition, so no clause is quoted. Registered at moderate on the strength of the inventory, which is distinctive, rather than the wording, which is not.

22:11.text: And the city was broken up, and all the men of war fled by night by the way of the gate between two walls, which is by the king’s garden: (now the Chaldees were against the city round about:) and the king went the way toward the plain.

provenance.other: “Fled by night” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Kings 25:4; “out of the city by night” occurs in exactly two, Jeremiah 39:4 and 52:7, the parallel accounts of the same night; “the army of the Chaldees pursued” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Kings 25:5, which also contains the singleton “overtook him in the plains”. tools/mediation-check.py on 2 Kings 25:4 against Jeremiah 52:7 returns one decisive point, for 2 Kings: the Book of Mormon has “toward” where Jeremiah has “of”. That discrimination should be leaned on lightly — the 1830 text reads “towards”, a form in no KJV verse at all — but it is the only point at which the two accounts differ over anything Mosiah reproduces.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's largest claim and the Book of Mormon supplies its own warrant for it. 2 Kings 25:4-5 is the flight of Zedekiah: the city broken up, the men of war escaping by night through a gate in the wall, the king making for open country, and the army of the Chaldees pursuing after him and overtaking him. Mosiah 22 runs the same five beats — a passage through the back wall of the city (22:6), a departure by night (22:11), a course bent toward open country, an army sent to pursue (22:15), and then the beat that does not match: “after they had pursued them two days, they could no longer follow their tracks; therefore they were lost in the wilderness” (22:16). The pursuers are the ones who get lost. Where Zedekiah is overtaken in the plains of Jericho and his army scattered from him, Limhi's people arrive. The reason this matters more than a good parallel is chronological. 1 Nephi 1:4 sets the whole Book of Mormon in motion “in the commencement of the first year of the reign of Zedekiah”, and three chapters after this escape, at Mosiah 25:2, the land the fugitives are running to turns out to have been founded by Mulek, a son of that same Zedekiah, brought out of Jerusalem when his father's flight failed. So a people escape a walled city by night, outrun the army sent after them, and reach the refuge of the one member of Zedekiah's house who got away. The book is rewriting its own founding catastrophe with the other ending.

22:11.note: “The people of king Limhi did depart by night into the wilderness with their flocks and their herds … and bent their course towards the land of Zarahemla.” Set against 2 Kings 25:4-5 the sequence is Zedekiah's: a way out through the wall, a flight by night, a course toward open country, an army in pursuit. The KJV's “fled by night” is a singleton belonging to that verse and “the army of the Chaldees pursued” is a singleton belonging to the next; Mosiah reproduces neither exactly, which keeps this at moderate. What raises it above a generic escape story is the ending, which is inverted — the pursuit fails and the pursuers are the ones lost in the wilderness — and the destination, since Mosiah 25:2 will say that Zarahemla was founded by Zedekiah's surviving son. The catalogue records the shape and leaves the reader to decide whether a writer built it or found it.
22:11.whyNot: The verbal contact is the weakest part of the row: no clause is reproduced, and every element considered separately — flight by night, a city wall, a pursuing army — is common in both scripture and life. A reader could hold that this is simply what an escape narrative looks like, and that the Zedekiah resonance is supplied by the Book of Mormon's own chronology rather than by any borrowing from 2 Kings. The row would be withdrawn if the sequence could be shown to follow some other escape account as closely; none of the KJV's others (Jacob from Laban, David from Saul, the men of Ai, Paul over the wall at Damascus) has both the night departure through the wall and the failed pursuit.
